addressed_problems.content: The paper's findings on pruning convolutional neural networks with self-supervision are based exclusively on unstructured magnitude-based iterative pruning, where individual weights are removed according to their magnitude. It remains an open question whether these observations—namely that pruned masks obtained without labels match the quality of supervised pruning when randomly re-initialized, that self-supervised pruning preserves transfer performance across downstream tasks, and that winning-ticket initializations from self-supervised tasks are less effective than those from supervised tasks—generalize to structured pruning methods (e.g., filter or channel pruning). Structured pruning removes entire groups of weights (e.g., entire filters or channels), which may have different effects on the learned representation, the capacity of the subnetwork, and the transferability of features. Moreover, the interplay between structured pruning and self-supervised learning objectives, which are agnostic to downstream tasks, has not been explored. Future work is needed to determine whether the insights from unstructured magnitude-based pruning hold for broader classes of pruning algorithms, including structured approaches and alternative scoring or optimization-based compression schemes.

The paper identifies that winning-ticket initializations obtained from self-supervised pruning are particularly sensitive to the choice of the late resetting (rewind) parameter—the point in training to which weights are reset before re-training the subnetwork. The notion of 'early in training' is ill-defined across different training setups: the amount of information learned in the early phase varies with dataset size, total number of epochs, mini-batch size, and learning rate schedule. In the paper, the rewind parameter was set to 3 × 1,280,000 samples for all ImageNet experiments, which corresponds to 3 epochs on full ImageNet but to 30 epochs on a 10% subset, leading to inconsistent criteria across settings. This sensitivity raises an open methodological question: how can a principled and standardized rewind criterion be defined that ensures fair, reproducible, and comparable evaluations of winning-ticket initializations across different datasets, training configurations, and pruning methods? Addressing this is essential for disentangling the effects of the mask from the effects of the weight initialization in lottery ticket studies.

The paper reveals a significant caveat when pruning deep neural networks on small-scale datasets such as CIFAR-10: a large fraction of the weights (e.g., ~80% of a ResNet-18 and ~85% of a VGG-19) naturally converge to zero during training, even without any pruning. This dataset-induced sparsity makes unstructured pruning at rates below this natural sparsity level trivial, because pruning simply zeros out weights that are already nearly zero. Consequently, pruning performance comparisons at moderate to high rates (e.g., below 80% sparsity) can be misleading: the apparent gain from pruning may reflect this natural sparsity rather than the effectiveness of the pruning algorithm. The paper proposed a corrected random baseline that first removes naturally zero weights, but this adjustment is not standard. It remains an open problem how to design evaluation protocols and benchmarks that account for dataset-dependent natural sparsity, so that pruning experiments reflect algorithmic improvements rather than artifacts of the training data. Standardized corrections—such as measuring and reporting the natural sparsity level of the trained network, adjusting baselines accordingly, and defining meaningful pruning regimes—are needed to ensure that conclusions about pruning methods are valid across different datasets and architectures.

Convolutional neural networks (convnets) pretrained without labels using self-supervised "pretext" tasks are increasingly competitive with supervised ImageNet pretraining, but these unsupervised convnets are often highly over-parameterized (sometimes hundreds of millions of weights). A standard remedy in supervised settings is pruning (removing weights or setting them to zero) to reduce parameter count and computational cost, typically carried out so as to preserve validation performance on the supervised training task. However, in self-supervised learning the training objective is an artificial proxy that does not explicitly encode the downstream supervised tasks for which the learned representations will later be transferred. Prior work on pruning has therefore focused almost exclusively on supervised objectives (and on specific pruning algorithms such as unstructured magnitude-based iterative pruning and variants of the lottery ticket rewinding procedure), leaving an unresolved question: whether pruning algorithms tuned to preserve performance on a pretext (self-supervised) objective will preserve the transferability of the resulting subnetworks and whether masks or initializations obtained without labels remain useful for supervised downstream training. Because preserving the pretext-task loss does not logically guarantee preservation of features useful for downstream tasks, there is a scientific gap: researchers lack empirical and methodological knowledge about (1) how standard pruning methods behave when the pruning objective is self-supervised rather than supervised, (2) whether label-agnostic pruned masks can be re-trained or fine-tuned on labeled data to reach competitive supervised accuracy, and (3) whether subtleties of pruning (choice of rewind/“winning-ticket” initialization, per-layer depth of pruning, dataset natural sparsity) qualitatively change conclusions about transferability. These limitations prevent confident use and distribution of already-pruned self-supervised pretrained models for downstream supervised tasks, and they leave open whether pruning can safely reduce compute for unsupervised pretraining without harming representational transfer.

nodes.content: In the practical setting of visual representation learning, researchers want to reduce the computation and memory cost of large self-supervised pretrained convnets while preserving the utility of their learned features for downstream tasks such as object or scene classification. Prior pruning work has primarily aimed to preserve performance on the same supervised training task used during pruning; because self-supervised pretext objectives are only proxy tasks, it was unknown whether masks and sparsified representations that preserve the pretext loss would also preserve downstream linear-transfer performance. Without such knowledge, practitioners cannot safely prune pretrained unsupervised models for release or deployment, since preserved pretext-task performance might mask degradation in transfer utility and thereby lead to degraded downstream performance or wasted computational effort.

A realistic workflow for resource-constrained users is to obtain an already-pruned pretrained model and then fine-tune it on a target task without performing further expensive pruning. However, a plausible alternative is to transfer an unpruned pretrained model and prune it during fine-tuning on the target labels, which directly optimizes the target objective under sparsity constraints. The unresolved question is which strategy better preserves target accuracy while minimizing user-side computation and complexity. If pruned pretrained models degrade target performance relative to pruning during transfer, releasing pruned pretrained models would impose a trade-off and limit their utility to low-resource users.

For model compression and reuse, it is necessary not only to identify a sparse architecture (mask $m\in\{0,1\}^d$) but also to know whether that sparse architecture can be trained effectively for a supervised downstream task. Prior supervised pruning work introduced the lottery ticket idea that both mask and a specific early-in-training weight state can be critical to re-training success. It was unknown whether label-agnostic pruning produces masks and initializations that are practically useful for supervised tasks: if self-supervised masks were poor, then pruning without labels would be of limited utility for downstream supervised training; if masks were good but initializations were poor, users would need to reinitialize differently. Clarifying whether mask quality and initialization quality transfer from self-supervision is therefore necessary to decide whether one can produce and distribute pruned unlabeled pretrained models that users can fine-tune for supervised tasks.

In transfer learning and pruning, different network depths encode different levels of abstraction; lower convolutional layers often capture general visual features while higher layers are more task-specific. If self-supervised pretraining yields weaker high-level semantic features, then pruning decisions that remove parameters in deeper layers may disproportionately harm the utility of self-supervised winning-ticket initializations. Understanding the layerwise sensitivity of self-supervised vs supervised pruning is important for devising pruning schemes that preserve transferability — for instance, whether to preferentially prune early layers or to apply different pruning strategies per depth — and for predicting when self-supervised masks and initializations will be adequate for downstream supervised training.

Purely label-agnostic pruning may produce masks whose architectures are useful but whose inherited early-in-training weight values do not optimally encode task-specific information for supervised downstream training. If a small amount of labeled data can substantially improve the inherited initialization without requiring full supervised pruning on all data, then semi-supervised pruning offers a practical compromise for generating pruned pretrained models for broader reuse. The open methodological question is how much label access is necessary and how it should be distributed across classes to produce reusable winning-ticket initializations; empirical evidence was needed to guide such semi-supervised pruning practices.

Many pruning studies evaluate methods on small datasets like CIFAR-10, but if networks trained on such datasets already become sparse at convergence, then iterative magnitude pruning may appear to succeed trivially by removing weights that had already decayed to zero. This natural sparsity confounds comparisons between pruning algorithms and baselines: without correcting for it, experiments can misattribute good post-pruning accuracy to the pruning algorithm rather than to the dataset-induced sparsity. For rigorous evaluation of pruning methods intended for large-scale settings, it is therefore necessary to detect and correct for dataset-dependent natural sparsity to avoid drawing misleading inferences about pruning performance.

For networks pretrained with self-supervised tasks RotNet (rotation prediction) or Exemplar (instance-based classification), applying unstructured magnitude-based iterative pruning to the pretrained convnet and then evaluating the pruned representation by training linear classifiers on downstream datasets yields that pruning up to approximately 90% of weights (i.e. retaining ≈10% of weights) does not significantly deteriorate linear-transfer performance on Pascal VOC 2007, Places205 and ImageNet linear evaluation; in some cases (RotNet and Exemplar) moderate pruning yields a slight improvement in transfer metrics, whereas severe pruning below roughly 5% remaining weights causes a substantial drop in transfer quality.

metadata.narrative: The derivation rests entirely on direct linear evaluation of pruned representations on three downstream datasets (VOC07, Places205, ImageNet). No load-bearing uncertainties were identified within the paper's scoped claim (linear-transfer performance on these datasets under the tested pruning method and self-supervised objectives). The evidence is straightforward and competently presented; the conclusion is well-supported for the tested conditions.

nodes.title: Pruning self-supervised pretraining preserves transfer feature quality up to high sparsity

nodes.content: When transferring a self-supervised pretrained convnet to a supervised target (Pascal VOC07) and fully fine-tuning all network parameters, using a network that was pruned during the self-supervised pretraining phase (i.e. the pruned pretrained model is used as initialization and then all parameters are fine-tuned) yields higher downstream accuracy than performing pruning while fine-tuning directly on the target supervised objective (pruning during transfer).

metadata.narrative: The primary risk is P1, which questions whether the comparison between pruning-during-pretraining and pruning-during-transfer is equally optimized for both strategies; the reported advantage could partly reflect hyperparameter asymmetry. H1 partially mitigates this by showing consistency across two self-supervised methods, indicating the effect is not driven by a single pretext task's peculiarities. However, no highlight directly addresses the hyperparameter sensitivity, so the risk remains partially unprotected. The conclusion is moderately credible but would benefit from a sensitivity analysis that tunes each strategy independently.

nodes.title: Finetuning a pruned pretrained network outperforms pruning during transfer

nodes.content: Masks obtained by iterative magnitude-based pruning performed on self-supervised pretraining (RotNet or Exemplar) define sparse subnetworks that, when re-trained from random re-initialization, reach ImageNet and CIFAR-10 supervised accuracies comparable to subnetworks obtained by supervised pruning (i.e. random re-initialization of self-supervised masks matches supervised-pruned random-reinit performance). However, when using the "winning tickets" rewind initialization (resetting the retained parameters to their early-in-training values), subnetworks pruned with labels exhibit substantially better re-training performance than subnetworks pruned with self-supervised objectives; consequently, the pruned mask m (the binary sparsity pattern) from self-supervision is of similar quality to supervised masks, but the inherited early-in-training weight values $W$ from self-supervised pretraining are not as effective initializations for supervised re-training as those inherited from supervised pruning.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion has two components: mask quality is similar between self-supervised and supervised pruning, and initialization quality differs. H2 strongly supports the mask-quality component by replicating it across four architectures. P2 introduces uncertainty about the initialization-difference component: if the rewind parameter were varied, the gap might narrow or disappear. No highlight protects against P2, so the initialization-difference claim remains vulnerable. The mask-quality conclusion is robust, while the initialization-difference conclusion is more fragile and rests on a single rewind choice.

nodes.title: Self-supervised pruning yields masks that can be re-trained on labels; mask quality similar to supervised pruning but winning-ticket initializations differ

nodes.content: Comparing winning-ticket initializations (rewind-to-early-training weights) obtained by pruning with labels versus pruning with self-supervised RotNet shows that the performance gap is small when pruning only early convolutional layers but increases substantially when pruning higher-level layers (e.g., when pruning through MLP/classifier layers), consistent with the observation that many self-supervised methods learn strong low- and mid-level features but comparatively weaker high-level semantic features needed for label classification.

metadata.narrative: The empirical observation that the gap increases with pruning depth is directly shown in Figure 4 for ResNet-50 and replicated for AlexNet in supplementary (H3). No load-bearing uncertainties were identified within the scoped claim. The conclusion is well-supported.

nodes.title: Difference between supervised and self-supervised winning-ticket initializations increases with pruning depth (higher layers)

nodes.content: Incorporating a small fraction of labeled data into the pruning/training process improves the quality of inherited initializations: using approximately 10% of ImageNet labels during pruning (either as simple supervised pruning on the 10% subset or via the S4L semi-supervised RotNet variant that combines RotNet and label loss) yields pruned subnetworks whose winning-ticket initializations re-trained on full ImageNet reach higher validation accuracy than purely unsupervised pruning. Among these, the S4L semi-supervised pruning (combining RotNet and labels on 10% of data) provides better resulting initializations than using 10% labels alone or purely unsupervised pruning, and sampling labeled data per class (keeping all classes represented) yields different effects than sampling a subset of classes, indicating winning-ticket initializations are somewhat task- or class-distribution dependent.

metadata.narrative: H4 provides a controlled ablation across multiple label conditions, clearly showing the ordering of initialization quality and the additional benefit of the semi-supervised combination. No load-bearing uncertainties were identified within the scoped claim (specific methods and dataset tested). The conclusion is well-supported for the tested semi-supervised method (S4L RotNet) and label proportions.

nodes.title: Limited label supervision during pruning improves winning-ticket initializations; semi-supervised pruning performs best

nodes.content: For common deep architectures trained on CIFAR-10 (e.g., VGG-19, ResNet-18), a large fraction of weights converge to zero during standard training (approximately 84.5% for VGG-19 and 80.3% for ResNet-18 in the reported experiments), so applying magnitude-based pruning at rates below this natural sparsity simply removes weights that were already zero and therefore can be trivially accomplished without affecting accuracy; consequently, random global pruning baselines must be adjusted to account for this natural sparsity when evaluating pruning on small datasets to avoid misleading conclusions.

metadata.narrative: P3 raises a measurement uncertainty about the threshold used to define zero weights; the precise sparsity percentages could shift under a less stringent threshold. However, H5 demonstrates the qualitative phenomenon across multiple architectures, supporting the general observation that networks trained on CIFAR-10 exhibit substantial natural sparsity. The quantitative numbers should be interpreted with caution, but the qualitative warning about trivial pruning remains credible. The baseline correction applied in Figure 3 is a methodological strength that increases confidence in the CIFAR-10 pruning experiments despite the threshold ambiguity.

nodes.title: Deep networks trained on small datasets (CIFAR-10) exhibit high natural sparsity; pruning there can be trivial unless accounted for

nodes.content: On Pascal VOC07 classification, two strategies were compared: (A) pruning a self-supervised pretrained ResNet-50 during RotNet or Exemplar pretext training and then fine-tuning the pruned network on VOC07 labels, versus (B) fine-tuning an unpruned self-supervised pretrained network on VOC07 while simultaneously performing iterative magnitude-based pruning on the VOC07 label objective. Both strategies used identical hyperparameters: pruning schedule of 20% of remaining weights per iteration, late-resetting parameter of 3 ImageNet epochs (weights reset to values after 3 epochs of training from start of first pruning iteration), and fine-tuning protocol of 90 epochs with learning rate 0.01 decayed at epochs 50, 65, 80. It is unknown whether separate hyperparameter optimization for each strategy (e.g., different learning rates or pruning schedules) would have altered the comparison, as strategy B starts from an unpruned feature extractor and prunes during fine-tuning, which may require different hyperparameters.

metadata.failure_mode: If the pruning-during-transfer strategy (B) were separately tuned (e.g., a lower initial learning rate, a cosine decay schedule instead of step decay, or a different pruning frequency such as 10% per iteration), its performance could match or exceed that of strategy A. In that case, the quantitative advantage reported in Figure 2 would disappear, and the claim that 'finetuning a pruned pretrained network outperforms pruning during transfer' would be unsupported. The conclusion's real-world implication (that releasing already-pruned pretrained models is strictly better for user-side accuracy) would be weakened, as users might achieve comparable results by pruning on their own target data with appropriate hyperparameters.
metadata.weakness_reason: The fairness of the comparison rests on the assumption that the same hyperparameter configuration is near-optimal for both strategies. However, pruning during fine-tuning (strategy B) involves a fundamentally different optimization landscape: the network is being fine-tuned to a new dataset while simultaneously undergoing pruning, which can destabilize training and may benefit from smaller learning rates, more gradual pruning, or additional training epochs. The paper provides no sensitivity analysis or hyperparameter search to rule out that strategy B's lower reported accuracy (by ~2 mAP at 0.1 remaining weights for RotNet, Figure 2) is an artifact of suboptimal tuning rather than an inherent disadvantage. Without such evidence, the conclusion that strategy A yields 'higher downstream accuracy' is incompletely established.

nodes.title: Same hyperparameters used for both pruning strategies on Pascal VOC07

nodes.content: For the comparison of winning-ticket initializations obtained by supervised versus self-supervised (RotNet or Exemplar) pruning on full ImageNet with a ResNet-50, the late-resetting (rewind) parameter is fixed at 3 epochs of full ImageNet training (weights are reset to their values after 3 epochs of training from the start of the first pruning iteration). Winning tickets performance is sensitive to the choice of rewind value when pruning with a 10% subset of ImageNet labels, but sensitivity for full ImageNet self-supervised pruning was not tested. The definition of 'early in training' is arbitrary; the observed gap in top-1 validation accuracy between supervised and self-supervised winning tickets may change or disappear if a different rewind point were adopted.

metadata.failure_mode: If a different rewind parameter (e.g., 1 epoch or 10 epochs) were used, self-supervised winning tickets might perform as well as or better than supervised winning tickets. In that scenario, the conclusion that 'the inherited early-in-training weight values from self-supervised pretraining are not as effective initializations for supervised re-training as those from supervised pruning' would be falsified. The broader claim that mask quality is similar but initialization quality differs (Conclusion 3) would lose its main empirical support for the initialization-difference component. The subsequent depth analysis (Conclusion 4) and the semi-supervised experiments (Conclusion 5), which rely on the same rewind parameter, would also be affected.
metadata.weakness_reason: The late-resetting parameter is a critical modeling choice in the lottery-ticket protocol: it determines how much training information is preserved in the reset weights. The paper shows that varying the rewind parameter for the 10%-label case shifts winning-ticket accuracy by several percentage points (Fig. 7). Since the self-supervised and supervised training trajectories differ in learning rate, loss landscape, and convergence speed, the same rewind value (3 epochs) may correspond to different stages of feature development for each objective. The paper does not justify why 3 epochs is an appropriate common baseline, nor does it explore alternatives. The absence of sensitivity analysis for the full ImageNet setting leaves open the possibility that the observed gap is an artifact of this specific rewind choice.

nodes.title: Winning-ticket comparison sensitivity to rewind parameter

nodes.content: Deep networks (VGG-19, ResNet-18) trained on CIFAR-10 exhibit high natural sparsity: 84.5% of VGG-19 weights and 80.3% of ResNet-18 weights are zeroed at convergence. This measurement uses thresholding at 'machine precision value', but the exact numerical threshold is not specified. The sensitivity of the reported sparsity percentages to small variations in the threshold (e.g., 1e-4, 1e-5, 1e-6) was not tested, nor was it evaluated whether weights below such thresholds have a functional role in network output or can be pruned without loss. The claim that pruning at rates below this natural sparsity is 'trivial' depends on the threshold choice and on the assumption that weights near machine precision are genuinely irrelevant.

metadata.failure_mode: If a more practical threshold (e.g., 1e-5, corresponding to weights that are small but potentially prunable without impact) were used, the reported natural sparsity might be substantially lower (e.g., 50% instead of 80%). Then, pruning at moderate rates (e.g., 60–80% remaining) would not be trivially accomplished by removing already-zeroed weights. The adjusted random baseline in Figure 3 for CIFAR-10 experiments would be inaccurate, potentially overestimating the relative advantage of self-supervised and supervised pruning over the random baseline. The conclusions about pruning on CIFAR-10 across all experiments (including Conclusions 1, 3, 4) would be partially invalidated, because the baseline correction that accounts for natural sparsity would be flawed.
metadata.weakness_reason: Determining what constitutes a 'zero' weight is inherently ambiguous due to floating-point representation and numeric training. Machine precision for float32 is approximately 1e-7 relative, but the paper likely refers to absolute threshold near the smallest representable positive float (around 1e-45). Many weight values may fall in the range 1e-10 to 1e-40 and are functionally zero for storage purposes but differ in their significance for computation. The paper provides no rationale for the chosen threshold, no sensitivity analysis, and no evaluation of whether weights below an alternative threshold can be removed without accuracy loss. The reported percentages could be inflated (if the threshold is too tight) or deflated (if too loose). This uncertainty propagates directly into the conclusion that pruning at 60–80% on CIFAR-10 is trivial, and into the correction applied to the random baseline in Figure 3, which uses this natural-sparsity measurement to adjust the baseline.

nodes.title: Natural sparsity measurement threshold dependence on CIFAR-10

nodes.content: On Pascal VOC07 fine-tuning, the advantage of pruning during self-supervised pretraining over pruning during transfer (i.e., higher top-1 accuracy at equivalent pruning rates) is observed for both RotNet and Exemplar self-supervised pretrained ResNet-50 networks across the full range of pruning rates (from 20% to 99.9% weights pruned), as shown in Figure 2.

metadata.credit: The consistency across two different self-supervised methods (rotation prediction and instance discrimination) preempts the alternative explanation that the observed advantage arises from a single pretext task's peculiarities. This cross-method replication supports the qualitative direction of the conclusion (pruning-during-pretraining yields higher or equal downstream accuracy) even if the exact quantitative gap may vary. Without this consistency, the conclusion would be vulnerable to task-specific artifacts. The scope of credit is the qualitative ranking and the regime of moderate-to-high sparsity (up to 99% pruning), tested on VOC07.

nodes.title: Consistency across two self-supervised methods

nodes.content: For subnetworks pruned with self-supervised tasks (RotNet, Exemplar) and retrained on labels, the finding that randomly re-initialized self-supervised masks match supervised-mask performance, and that self-supervised winning tickets underperform supervised winning tickets, is consistently observed across four architectures: ResNet-50 (ImageNet), AlexNet (ImageNet), VGG-19 (CIFAR-10), and ResNet-18 (CIFAR-10), as reported in Figure 3 and supplementary Figure 8.

metadata.credit: The multi-architecture replication rules out the possibility that the observed mask-quality similarity and initialization-quality difference are idiosyncratic to a single network design (e.g., residual connections in ResNet). If the pattern held only for one architecture, the conclusion that self-supervised masks are generally re-trainable on labels would not be warranted. The replication across very different architectures (ResNets, VGG, AlexNet) with varying depths, widths, and training recipes underwrites the generalization of both components of the conclusion. The scope of credit is the qualitative directions (mask quality comparable, initialization quality worse) under the tested pruning method and rewind protocol.

nodes.title: Replication across multiple architectures

nodes.content: The observation that the performance gap between supervised and self-supervised winning tickets increases systematically as pruning extends to higher (deeper) layers is replicated for both ResNet-50 (Figure 4) and AlexNet (supplementary Figure 9), with AlexNet showing a particularly clear widening when the MLP layers are included.

metadata.credit: The replication across two distinct architectures (one with residual connections and one without) strengthens the claim that the depth-dependent gap is a general property of the relationship between self-supervised feature hierarchies and pruning, rather than an artifact of a specific architecture's layer organization. Without this cross-architecture evidence, the conclusion would rest on a single model (ResNet-50) and the interpretation about self-supervised high-level features would be less credible. The scope of credit is the qualitative trend (gap increases with depth) and the regime of unstructured magnitude pruning on ImageNet.

nodes.title: Cross-architecture replication of layerwise depth effect

nodes.content: On ImageNet with ResNet-50, the paper compares winning-ticket initialization quality (measured by retraining on full ImageNet labels) across five conditions: (1) purely unsupervised pruning (RotNet), (2) supervised pruning on 10% of labels sampled per class, (3) supervised pruning on 10% of labels sampled as a subset of classes, (4) semi-supervised pruning (S4L RotNet, which combines RotNet loss on all data with label loss on 10% per-class labels), and (5) fully supervised pruning on all labels. The relative ordering of these conditions is consistent across pruning rates (Figure 5).

metadata.credit: The systematic ablation design allows attribution of the improvement in initialization quality to the amount and distribution of labeled information. The ordering unsupervised < 10% labels (per class) < S4L < full labels preempts the alternative that any label presence trivially benefits pruning; instead, it shows a monotonic benefit that increases with the amount and relevance of label supervision, and that the semi-supervised combination outperforms pure 10% label training. Without this controlled comparison, the claim that semi-supervised pruning performs best would be less differentiated and the role of label distribution would be obscured. The scope of credit is the qualitative ordering within the tested methods and the per-class vs. subset-of-classes distinction.

nodes.title: Controlled ablation across multiple label-supervision conditions

nodes.content: The observation that networks trained on CIFAR-10 converge with a large fraction of zeroed weights is not limited to a single architecture: the paper reports sparsity percentages for VGG-19 (84.5%), ResNet-18 (80.3%), VGG-16 (72.8%), and AlexNet (64.2%) in supplementary Figure 10, using the same thresholding protocol.

metadata.credit: By replicating the natural-sparsity phenomenon across four common deep architectures (including both VGG-style and ResNet-style networks), the paper establishes that the effect is a general property of training large ImageNet-adapted architectures on the small CIFAR-10 dataset, not an isolated artifact of a specific model. This multi-architecture evidence supports the conclusion's applicability to typical pruning evaluations on CIFAR-10. Without this, the warning about trivial pruning could be dismissed as architecture-specific. The scope of credit is the qualitative existence of substantial natural sparsity and its quantitative range across architectures.

nodes.title: Multi-architecture demonstration of natural sparsity

steps.reasoning:
Define the pruning algorithm used: unstructured magnitude-based iterative pruning which alternates (a) training the network to convergence to obtain final weights $W^*$ and (b) updating a binary mask $m\in\{0,1\}^d$ by setting to zero the already-masked elements plus the smallest-magnitude remaining weights, thereby producing a pruned subnetwork represented by $(W,m)$ and a convnet function $f_{m\odot W}$ where $\odot$ denotes element-wise product; this is the pruning procedure applied throughout the experiments.
[8]

Specify the self-supervised pretext tasks used to obtain pretrained convnet weights $W$ before pruning: RotNet (predicting image rotation among $\{0^\circ,90^\circ,180^\circ,270^\circ\}$) and Exemplar (instance discrimination where each image and its transformations form a distinct class); these two methods are chosen because RotNet has a small output space encouraging discriminability to rotations while Exemplar has a large output space encouraging invariance to transformations.
[10]
[29]

Define the evaluation protocol for transfer quality of pruned self-supervised features: freeze the pruned convnet up to the penultimate layer to produce a representation vector (the penultimate-layer feature), then train linear classifiers on top of these representations for three downstream supervised tasks: Pascal VOC 2007 object classification (VOC07), Places205 scene classification (Places205), and ImageNet linear evaluation (ImageNet); performance of these linear classifiers is used as the metric of representation transfer quality.
[39]
[40]
[34]

Describe pruning schedule and implementation specifics that produced the pruned representations whose transfer quality is measured: at each pruning iteration globally remove 20% of remaining weights, leave the last fully-connected and batch-norm layers unpruned, and run up to 30 pruning iterations to obtain pruning rates spanning from 20% to 99.9% removed (i.e. remaining weights from 80% down to 0.1%); these settings generate the sequence of pruned models evaluated in transfer.

Report the empirical trend observed when varying pruning rate for RotNet and Exemplar self-supervised pretrained models: when training linear classifiers on pruned representations, pruning up to approximately 90% of weights removed (i.e. $\approx 10\%$ of weights remaining) does not deteriorate linear-transfer performance on Pascal VOC 2007, Places205 and ImageNet linear evaluation; in some cases (RotNet and Exemplar) moderate pruning yields a slight improvement in transfer metrics, consistent with the observed small increases in linear evaluation accuracy as pruning progresses up to that moderate-to-high sparsity regime.
Fig. 1

Record the contrasting empirical behaviors at extreme pruning: for the non-parametric instance discrimination method (NPID) the representation quality remains essentially constant at moderate pruning rates, and when pruning becomes severe so that less than roughly $5\%$ of weights remain, transfer quality of pruned representations drops substantially across methods, indicating a sharp degradation in representational power below that extreme sparsity point.
Fig. 1

Provide the authors' suggested interpretation of the slight improvements under moderate pruning: pruning may remove task-specific (pretext-task-specific) nuisance information from the features, thereby improving general transferability to downstream label tasks; this is offered as a plausible explanation rather than a proved mechanism.

Conclude from the above empirical observations that applying iterative magnitude-based unstructured pruning to convnets pretrained with self-supervised tasks (RotNet, Exemplar) preserves linear-transfer feature quality up to high sparsity (roughly 90% pruning / $\approx 10\%$ remaining), sometimes yields small improvements for moderate pruning, and that only very severe pruning (below $\sim 5\%$ remaining) causes a substantial drop in transfer performance.
Fig. 1

State the transfer scenario under study: use self-supervised pretrained features as weight initialization for a supervised downstream task (Pascal VOC07), then fully fine-tune all network parameters on the downstream supervised objective; compare two pruning regimes for producing the pruned model used at transfer time: (A) prune during pre-training on the self-supervised task and then fine-tune the pruned pretrained model on the supervised target, versus (B) prune during transfer by pruning while fine-tuning directly on the supervised target.

Describe the experimental protocol used to compare these two pruning regimes on Pascal VOC07: pretrained features are used as initialization and all network parameters are fine-tuned on VOC07 for 90 epochs using train+val splits, starting learning rate 0.01 decayed by factor 10 at epochs 50, 65 and 80; models are evaluated using the central-crop test metric reported for Pascal VOC07.
Fig. 2

Report the empirical observation from the comparison: when measuring final downstream supervised accuracy on Pascal VOC07 as a function of pruning rate, using a network that was pruned during the self-supervised pretraining phase and then fully fine-tuning its parameters yields higher downstream accuracy than performing pruning while fine-tuning directly on the supervised target (i.e. pruning during transfer achieves lower final accuracy than pruning during pre-training followed by full finetuning).
Fig. 2

Note the practical implication the authors draw from this empirical finding: it is advantageous to release already pruned pretrained models to end users because finetuning a pruned pretrained model on the users' target tasks gives better performance than requiring users to prune while fine-tuning; releasing pruned pretrained models therefore avoids additional pruning computations on the transfer task.

Conclude that fully fine-tuning a network that was pruned during self-supervised pretraining outperforms performing pruning during the transfer fine-tuning procedure on the supervised target, as demonstrated on Pascal VOC07 under the described training protocol.
Fig. 2

Starting point: accept as established the empirical fact that CIFAR-10 networks can be highly sparse at convergence (natural sparsity) which the authors used to adjust their random baselines when evaluating re-training of pruned masks on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet; this is the upstream result that informs interpretation of CIFAR-10 experiments in what follows.
Fig. 6

State the experiment to evaluate pruned masks and initializations obtained by pruning with self-supervised objectives: iterative magnitude-based pruning is applied during self-supervised pretraining (RotNet or Exemplar) to produce a mask $m\in\{0,1\}^d$ and an associated set of weights $W\in\mathbb{R}^d$; the authors then re-train the resulting sparse subnetwork $f_{m\odot W}$ on supervised label classification tasks under two initialization schemes for the retained weights: (a) "Random Reinit" where the retained parameters are randomly re-initialized before re-training, and (b) "Winning Tickets" where retained parameters are reset to their early-in-training values (rewind), following the lottery-ticket-style rewinding procedure.
[11]
[12]

Describe the comparison set: the experiments compare subnetworks obtained by self-supervised pruning ("RotNet" or "Exemplar") to subnetworks pruned with labels ("Labels") and to randomly pruned subnetworks ("Random") where masks are random permutations with random retained weight values; for CIFAR-10 the random baseline is adjusted to respect the natural sparsity discovered earlier.
Fig. 3

Report the empirical outcome when re-training pruned subnetworks from random re-initialization: on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 the authors observe that when the pruned subnetworks are re-trained from random re-initialization, the subnetworks whose masks were obtained via self-supervised pruning (RotNet or Exemplar) reach supervised accuracies that are comparable to subnetworks obtained by supervised pruning; in other words, the pruned mask $m$ coming from self-supervision is of similar quality to a supervised mask when the retained weights are randomly reinitialized prior to re-training.
Fig. 3

Report the empirical outcome when using winning-ticket ("rewind") initializations: when the retained parameters are reset to their early-in-training values (the "winning ticket" initialization), subnetworks pruned with supervised labels show substantially better re-training performance than subnetworks pruned with self-supervised objectives; specifically, supervised-pruned winning-ticket initializations yield a significant accuracy advantage over self-supervised-pruned winning-ticket initializations, while both remain above random-pruning performance.
Fig. 3

Synthesize the comparative insight: because random re-initialization makes self-supervised and supervised pruned subnetworks perform similarly when re-trained, whereas winning-ticket initializations expose a substantial advantage for supervised pruning, the authors conclude that the pruned mask $m$ obtained from self-supervision is of comparable quality to supervised masks in terms of architecture/sparsity pattern, but the inherited early-in-training weight values $W$ from self-supervised pretraining are not as effective as those inherited from supervised pruning when used as winning-ticket initializations for supervised re-training.
Fig. 3

Note the dependence on pruning severity: the gap between self-supervised and random pruning increases when the network is severely pruned (fewer remaining weights), and the deficit of self-supervised winning-ticket initializations relative to supervised winning-ticket initializations is especially visible at higher pruning rates, indicating the phenomenon is more pronounced under stronger sparsity constraints.
Fig. 3

Conclude that masks obtained by iterative magnitude-based pruning on self-supervised pretraining define sparse subnetworks that can be re-trained from random re-initialization to reach supervised accuracies comparable to supervised-pruned subnetworks, but that the winning-ticket (rewind) initializations inherited from self-supervised pretraining are substantially less effective for supervised re-training than winning tickets obtained from supervised pruning; therefore mask quality is similar while the inherited weight values $W$ differ in utility.

Start from the upstream result that self-supervised pruned masks and initializations have differing efficacy compared to supervised ones (conclusion that the mask quality is similar but winning-ticket initializations from self-supervision are weaker); treat this upstream conclusion as established for the present derivation.

Describe the layerwise pruning experiment: generate winning-ticket initializations by performing iterative magnitude-based pruning that only prunes the first $n$ convolutional layers of the network while leaving the remaining layers (including higher-level layers and the classifier/MLP) unpruned; vary $n$ to produce winning-ticket initializations that differ in the highest layer pruned, and evaluate the resulting subnetworks re-trained on ImageNet classification to measure how pruning depth affects the relative performance of supervised-pruned versus self-supervised-pruned winning tickets.
Fig. 4

Report the empirical observation: when pruning only the earliest convolutional layers (small $n$), the performance gap between winning-ticket initializations obtained by supervised pruning and those obtained by self-supervised (RotNet) pruning is small (the two initializations perform similarly when only early layers are pruned); however, when pruning proceeds to higher-level layers, in particular when pruning includes the MLP/classifier layers (larger $n$, up to pruning the whole network), the performance gap increases substantially with supervised winning tickets yielding higher re-training accuracy than self-supervised winning tickets.
Fig. 4

Connect the experimental result to an explanatory observation about self-supervised features: the increasing gap with pruning depth is consistent with prior observations that many self-supervised methods produce strong low- and mid-level features but comparatively weaker high-level semantic features needed for label classification; therefore pruning higher layers (which are more semantic) uncovers larger differences between the quality of supervised and self-supervised winning-ticket initializations.
[41]

Conclude that the difference in effectiveness between supervised and self-supervised winning-ticket initializations is small when pruning only early convolutional layers but increases substantially when pruning higher-level layers (e.g., including the classifier/MLP), supporting the interpretation that self-supervised methods learn relatively weaker high-level semantic features.
Fig. 4

Start from the upstream understanding that (a) pruned masks from self-supervision are of similar quality to supervised masks when re-trained from random initialization, but (b) winning-ticket initializations from supervised pruning produce better re-training performance than those from self-supervision; treat these established observations as premises for the semi-supervised pruning investigation.
Fig. 3

Describe the semi-supervised pruning experimental setups compared: use approximately $10\%$ of ImageNet labels in two sampling modes (i) sampling 10% images per class thereby preserving class coverage, and (ii) sampling 10% of classes and keeping all images of those classes (reducing class diversity); evaluate three pruning regimes that leverage limited labels: (A) supervised pruning on the 10% labeled subset only ("10% Lab"), (B) semi-supervised pruning using the S4L RotNet variant that combines the RotNet self-supervised loss on all data plus a classification loss on labeled examples ("S4L"), and (C) purely unsupervised pruning with RotNet on the unlabeled dataset ("RotNet"); for reference also include full-supervision pruning ("Labels") and random pruning baselines.
[42]

Specify the evaluation methodology for resulting pruned masks and initializations: after producing masks and corresponding winning-ticket initializations under each pruning regime, re-train the resulting subnetworks on full ImageNet supervised classification and report validation top-1 accuracy as a measure of winning-ticket initialization quality.
Fig. 5

Report the empirical findings: (a) adding $10\%$ labels for pruning via the S4L semi-supervised method yields substantially improved winning-ticket initialization performance upon re-training on full ImageNet compared to purely unsupervised RotNet pruning; (b) performing supervised pruning using only 10% of labeled images ("10% Lab") also yields better winning-ticket initializations than unsupervised pruning (RotNet), indicating that limited labels help; and (c) the semi-supervised S4L approach generally outperforms both the pure 10% supervised pruning and pure unsupervised pruning, producing the best resulting initializations among the limited-label regimes.
Fig. 5

Report the observed dependence on how labeled data are sampled: the performance gap between limited-label pruning and unsupervised pruning is wider when the 10% labeled subset preserves all classes (i.e. sampling images per class) than when the labeled subset reduces class diversity (i.e. sampling only a subset of classes), suggesting that winning-ticket initializations depend to some extent on the task or class-distribution used during pruning.
Fig. 5

Provide the interpretive synthesis based on the upstream result about mask versus initialization: since earlier results showed that pruned masks are similar in quality between supervised and unsupervised pruning, the authors attribute the improvements from adding limited labels mainly to producing better winning-ticket (rewind) initializations rather than dramatically different mask patterns; semi-supervised pruning likely captures complementary statistics (label signal plus self-supervised invariances) that jointly yield better initializations.
Fig. 3
Fig. 5

Conclude that incorporating a small fraction of labeled data (about 10% of ImageNet) into the pruning/training process improves the quality of inherited winning-ticket initializations, with semi-supervised pruning (S4L RotNet plus labels) producing better initializations than supervised pruning on 10% labels alone or purely unsupervised pruning, and that sampling labeled data per class versus sampling a subset of classes yields different effects indicating some task- or class-distribution dependence of winning-ticket initializations.

Define the empirical phenomenon under investigation: measure the distribution and magnitudes of trained network weights at convergence for deep architectures trained on small dataset CIFAR-10 and compare to ImageNet-trained networks, with the goal of determining whether a substantial fraction of weights naturally go to zero during standard training (termed "natural sparsity").

Describe the experimental observation reported: for a VGG-19 network trained on CIFAR-10 the authors observe approximately $ \sim 84.5\%$ of the weights at convergence are numerically zero, and for a ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 approximately $ \sim 80.3\%$ of the weights at convergence are numerically zero when thresholding at machine-precision-level values; this high proportion of zeroed weights is not observed to the same extent in ImageNet-trained networks.
Fig. 6

Explain the consequence of this natural sparsity for pruning experiments on CIFAR-10: applying magnitude-based pruning at rates below this natural sparsity (i.e. removing up to $\sim 80\%$ or more of weights) is trivial because many weights have already converged to zero and pruning simply freezes out weights that were already zero, hence such pruning does not meaningfully change the model or its accuracy; unstructured magnitude-based pruning can therefore act like training rather than compression in this regime.
[22]

Describe how this observation affects baseline design and evaluation: a naive global random pruning baseline that removes (potentially) non-zero weights will degrade accuracy at pruning rates below the natural sparsity, whereas pruning weights that are already zero has no effect; to obtain a fair random-baseline comparison on CIFAR-10, the authors correct for natural sparsity by first removing the weights that converged to zero and then randomly masking among the remaining non-zero weights to reach desired final pruning rates; this adjusted baseline is used in subsequent comparisons (e.g. in Figure 3).
Fig. 3

Conclude that deep networks trained on small datasets such as CIFAR-10 can exhibit high natural sparsity (e.g. $\sim 84.5\%$ for VGG-19 and $\sim 80.3\%$ for ResNet-18 in the experiments), making pruning at rates below this level trivial and necessitating baseline adjustments to avoid misleading conclusions when evaluating pruning on small datasets.
Fig. 6

open_questions.content: The study acknowledges several unresolved scientific issues and limitations that remain to be investigated: (1) The experiments consider only unstructured magnitude-based iterative pruning; it is unresolved whether the empirical observations (mask transferability, re-trainability, behavior of winning-ticket initializations) generalize to other pruning paradigms, especially structured pruning methods (e.g. filter/channel pruning) and alternative scoring or optimization-based compression schemes. (2) Winning-ticket initializations are sensitive to the choice of the rewind or "late resetting" parameter (the epoch or number of samples/updates to which weights are reset), and the notion of what constitutes "early in training" is ill-defined across datasets, batch sizes and schedules; it remains an open methodological question how to define and standardize rewind criteria so that winning-ticket comparisons across settings are fair and reproducible. (3) The natural sparsity of networks trained on small datasets (e.g. CIFAR-10) complicates interpretation of pruning experiments; it remains to be determined how best to correct baselines and design benchmarks so that pruning evaluations reflect algorithmic gain rather than dataset-induced sparsity. These limitations point to concrete future work: testing other pruning algorithms (including structured methods), systematically studying rewind/rewind-criterion effects across tasks and scales, and establishing standardized evaluation protocols that account for dataset-dependent natural sparsity.
